transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I... I suppose what brings me in is just this awful feeling in my head lately. It's like my brain is full of cotton wool, or fog, or something. Just completely cloudy. I've been managing properties and homeowner associations for years—decades, really—and I've always been sharp. I had to be, you know? But lately, I'll sit down at my desk, and I'll pull up a board packet for the upcoming monthly meeting, or maybe just a simple email from one of our landscaping vendors asking about the sprinkler schedule, and I just stare at it. I stare at the words and I can't... I just can't make a decision. Things that used to take me two seconds, things I could do in my sleep, are suddenly impossible. I'll read the same paragraph over and over, and my mind just won't process it. It's so frustrating because I know I should be able to handle it, but I just sit there, staring at the screen, completely stuck.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Depressed... well, I don't really know if I'd call it that. I just... I'm not sure. I mean, I guess I feel bad about myself, but wouldn't anyone in my shoes? It’s just... well, let me explain it like this. I’ve been working since I was a young girl. I didn't even make it past the eighth grade, you know, I had to go right out and work to help my family, and I built my whole life up from nothing. I worked my way up to where I am now, and I’m proud of that. I handle huge budgets and important decisions for these communities. 

So when I sit at my desk and I can't even figure out if we should approve a simple, everyday repair for a community pool gate... it’s upsetting. It really is. I just sit there and wonder what on earth is wrong with me. I don't know if that means I'm depressed in the medical way you doctors mean. I'm just so incredibly frustrated with this cloud in my head. It makes me feel... well, just useless, really. I go home and I just think about all the things I didn't get done. Like yesterday, a resident was asking about her parking spot, and usually I'd just handle it in a snap, but I just stared at the screen, and then I went home and just sat there feeling awful about it all evening. So, am I depressed? I really couldn't tell you for sure. I just know I don't feel right.
Have you been forgetting recent conversations or appointments?

No, no, it's not like that. I'm not forgetting things. My memory is fine, thank goodness. I mean, I can still remember all the bylaws for the different associations I manage, and I know exactly who called me yesterday and what they said. Like Mrs. Higgins in unit 4B, she called about her neighbor's dog barking again, and I remember every word of that conversation. And my appointments, well, I have my calendar right there on my desk, but I don't even really need to look at it most days. I know when my meetings are. 

It's just... it's the *doing* of the things that's the problem. I remember that I need to call the roofer about the leak at the Oakwood property, I know the appointment is at 2:00 PM, I remember the conversation I had with the board president about it, but when the time comes to actually pick up the phone and make the decision on the estimate... that's when the fog rolls in. I just sit there. So the memory is all there, clear as a bell. It's just the rest of my brain that feels like it's wading through molasses. I'll remember that I sat there for an hour getting nothing done, which just makes me feel worse, you know? But no, no lost time or forgotten conversations. Just this awful inability to act on what I remember.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Well, yes, actually. And that's another thing that's been bothering me so much. You see, I've always been a very active person outside of work, too. For years, I've gone to this wonderful little dance class on Thursday evenings. It's just a local group, mostly ladies my age, and we do a bit of everything—some line dancing, a little ballroom, just moving around and having a good time. It’s always been the highlight of my week. I’d get off work, maybe grab a quick bite, and head straight there. But lately... I just can't bring myself to go. The thought of putting on my shoes and driving over there just feels like climbing a mountain. I haven't been in weeks. 

And it's not just the dancing. On the weekends, I usually love to stroll downtown and look at the little art galleries. I don't always buy anything, but I love seeing what the local artists are doing, chatting with the gallery owners—I know most of them by name now. It’s a lovely way to spend a Saturday afternoon. But now, the idea of getting dressed and walking around just seems exhausting. I’d rather just sit in my chair at home. 

Even Sunday dinners... oh, that's the hardest part. I've always cooked a big Sunday meal for my family. My kids and grandkids come over, and I make a roast, or sometimes a big pot of my mother's famous chicken and dumplings. I love the house smelling like good food, hearing everyone laughing in the living room while I’m finishing up the gravy. It's what makes me feel like *me*, you know? The matriarch, taking care of everyone. But the last few Sundays, I've just told them I wasn't up to it. I couldn't even fathom the idea of planning a menu, going to the grocery store, standing at the stove for hours... It just feels so heavy. So, yes, I suppose I have lost interest. All the things that usually bring me joy, that make me feel alive and like myself... they just feel like chores now, and I just don't have the energy or the desire for them anymore.
Have you been feeling slowed down physically, like your body is moving through molasses?

Well, it's funny you should put it exactly that way, because yes, sometimes I do feel just like that—like I'm moving through molasses. But it's not all the time, and that's what makes it so confusing for me. 

When I'm at home, especially in the evenings after work or on those weekends when I just can't bring myself to go out to the galleries, it's like my legs are made of lead. Getting up from my chair in the living room to just go to the kitchen for a glass of water feels like such an enormous effort. I move so slowly, dragging my feet across the carpet, and I just feel physically heavy. I'll tell myself, 'Come on, just stand up,' and it takes me five minutes to actually do it. It's like my body just doesn't want to cooperate with what little bit of will I have left. 

But then... then there are other times, mostly at work, where it's the exact opposite. And this is what I don't understand. I'll be in one of those board meetings—you know, the ones where we have to discuss the annual budgets or deal with a difficult contractor—and I just can't seem to settle down. I'll be sitting there, and I catch myself tapping my pen on the notepad, just tap-tap-tap, until one of the board members gives me a look. Or I'm shifting my weight in the chair, crossing and uncrossing my legs, adjusting my posture every two minutes. I feel so keyed up, almost like there's an electric current running under my skin, and I just can't sit still to save my life. It's not a good kind of energy, though; it's this uncomfortable, restless feeling. 

So it's both, really. Heavy and slow like molasses when I'm alone in my house, but then all jittery and wound up tight when I'm trying to sit through a meeting. It makes no sense to me. How can a person be too exhausted to walk to the kitchen, but too restless to sit in a chair at the office? It's just exhausting in a whole different way, dealing with this back-and-forth.
Have you been having thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

Oh, heavens... that’s... well, that’s a very hard question to hear out loud. But, to be completely honest with you, because I know I need to be... there have been a few mornings lately. 

You know, it's usually right when the sun is just starting to peek through the gaps in the blinds in my bedroom, right before my alarm is even set to go off. I’ll just be lying there, looking up at the ceiling fan, thinking about everything I have to do that day—the emails from the association board, the contractors I need to wrangle, and just the sheer effort of putting my feet on the floor. And... well, I’ve had this really scary thought creep in. Just a flash, really, but it frightens me so much. I catch myself thinking that maybe... maybe it would just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. If I could just stay asleep and not have to face the day or this awful, heavy feeling anymore. 

It terrifies me to even admit that to you, because I’ve always been such a strong person, you know? I'm the one holding it all together, the matriarch, like I said. But I need you to know—and I tell myself this right after the thought happens—I do not want to hurt myself. Oh, Lord, no. I could never, ever do that. I think about my kids, and my grandchildren, and the thought of leaving them that way, of putting them through that kind of pain... it breaks my heart to even imagine it. So, no, I don't have any sort of plan or anything like that. I'm not going to do anything to harm myself, I promise you that. It's just... it's just that fleeting, frightening wish that I could just peacefully not wake up, just so I wouldn't have to push through the day anymore.
Have these problems been going on for at least two weeks?

Well, let me think about the exact timing, because I do try to keep track of when things start feeling off. It’s been... yes, it’s been right around two weeks. I know this for a fact because it all really started to shift right when my husband retired. 

He just officially retired two weeks ago, you see. After all these years of him going off to work every single morning, suddenly he is just... home. All day long. And bless his heart, I love him dearly, we've been married a long time, but having him underfoot from dawn until dusk has been such a huge adjustment. I’m used to having my mornings to myself, getting my association paperwork sorted out at the dining room table in peace, and now he’s wandering around the kitchen asking what’s for lunch at ten in the morning, or sitting in his recliner watching his programs with the volume turned way up. 

It was right around that exact time, two weeks ago, that I noticed this sharper change in myself. At first, I had this shift in my energy and my confidence, like I was trying to manage everything and everyone all at once and feeling so wound up. But then, almost right on the heels of that, came this... this low, cloudy feeling. That heavy, exhausting feeling I was telling you about earlier. So, yes, doctor, it’s been a solid two weeks of this. Ever since he was suddenly home all day, it just feels like my whole routine got turned upside down, and this awful cloudy feeling settled right in over me.
Do you feel these symptoms started because of your husband retiring and being home all day?

Well, now that you ask it quite like that, I suppose I should clarify a bit. I don't want to lay all the blame on my dear husband, heaven knows. It's not quite that simple. 

You see, if I'm being perfectly honest and looking back over the calendar... these low periods, these stretches where everything feels like wading through that molasses I mentioned, they've actually been coming and going for a while now. I'd say it's been happening on and off for about a year. I remember last Thanksgiving feeling just so dreadful and hollow while trying to get the turkey in the oven, and then again around Easter when I couldn't even bring myself to arrange the centerpieces for the association luncheon. So, the cloudy feeling itself isn't entirely new. 

But... and this is the important part, I think... this particular stretch, the one I'm in right now, it definitely feels like it was triggered or maybe just made so much worse by his retirement. It’s like the stress of him suddenly being in my space all day, disrupting my peace and quiet and my routines... it just flipped a switch. So while the depressed stretches have been creeping up on me for a year or so, this latest, heavy bout—the one that's kept me down for the last two weeks—feels entirely tied to the upheaval of him stopping work and being home from dawn to dusk. It just pushed me right back down into that hole, you know?
Before this current spell, have you had another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?

Well, yes, absolutely. If I really sit down and look at the calendar, they definitely last that long, if not longer. Like I mentioned a moment ago with Thanksgiving... that wasn't just a bad weekend or a fleeting mood. Oh, heavens no. I felt that awful, heavy way from the very first week of November all the way through to early December. I remember it so clearly because the community association always does a canned food drive right around then, and I am usually the one organizing the collection bins down at the clubhouse, making sure the flyers are distributed to all the units. But last year, I just couldn't muster the energy for weeks on end. I had to have Mrs. Gable from unit 4B handle the whole thing, which I hated doing, but I just couldn't get out of bed some days. 

It was the exact same story around Easter, too. It just dragged on and on for well over a month before the clouds finally parted. So, yes, to answer your question, these depressed stretches, they have been coming back on and off for about a year now, and when they do settle in, they certainly overstay their welcome for at least two weeks, sometimes much longer. 

But I just have to say again, because it's weighing on me so heavily right now... even though this has been happening for a year, this latest one feels so much more tied to what happened after my husband stopped working. It's like the other times were just a terrible season I had to wait out, but this time, him being home all day, asking me questions while I'm trying to balance the association ledger, changing the channel on the television when I'm trying to have a moment of quiet... it just brought the storm right into my living room, if that makes sense. So yes, they do last a long time, but this one just feels so specifically wrapped up in his retirement.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually energetic or needed much less sleep than usual?

Well, yes... yes, actually. I don't know if I'd say I needed less sleep, but the energy... oh, heavens, the energy. It was like I had this... this push inside my body, just this constant hum, like I had to keep moving every single second. 

It happened... oh, I guess it was a few months ago now. I was just going a mile a minute. I’d be up and I just couldn't sit still. I was calling everyone on the association board, sometimes two or three times a day, just rapid-fire, going over the landscaping budget, the pool maintenance schedule, making these huge, elaborate lists of every little thing that needed fixing in the whole community. I mean, page after page of lists. And I wouldn't just stop at the paperwork, no. I was out walking the properties, inspecting the common areas, checking the sprinkler heads, looking at the paint on the carports... and I'd be doing this long after I should have just gone home and put my feet up. 

I remember one evening, it must have been past seven o'clock, getting dark, and there I was, marching around the perimeter fence with my clipboard, just feeling like I could keep going all night. It wasn't like this heavy, cloudy feeling at all, it was the exact opposite. Just this driven, almost frantic need to do things, fix things, organize things. I was exhausted underneath it all, I think, but my body just wouldn't get the message to stop. It was quite a change from how I usually am, I must say.
During that unusually energetic period a few months ago, did you need less sleep than usual?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about the sleep specifically, because when I was rushing around like that, making all those lists and checking the sprinkler heads and calling the board members... I honestly can't say for sure if I actually *needed* less sleep. It wasn't like I was staying up until three in the morning baking pies or anything like that. 

I mean, I still went to bed around my usual time, maybe a little later because my mind was just racing with all the things I still had to do for the association, like whether we should switch from pine straw to mulch around the clubhouse. But I don't recall waking up at the crack of dawn feeling completely refreshed on just a few hours of sleep, if that's what you mean. 

It was more that while I was awake, I just couldn't turn the motor off. I was just going and going. But as for the sleep itself... I really don't think I was sleeping significantly less than I usually do. Or at least, I didn't notice it if I was. I was just so focused on getting everything done, you see. I suppose I was probably still getting my normal seven or eight hours, just... tossing and turning a bit more before I finally drifted off. So, no, I don't think the sleep part was really the issue, just the non-stop doing things during the day.
During that high-energy period a few months ago, did you feel unusually cheerful or overly confident?

Well, cheerful is a funny word for it, but... oh, I suppose there were days during that stretch where I felt, I don't know, almost too bright? Too bold, maybe. Like I was just on top of the world and nobody could tell me otherwise. 

I remember at one of the association meetings—it was the one where we were discussing the new paint colors for the carports, which is always a contentious issue, let me tell you—I was just holding court. I was talking over people, which I never do, I'm usually very polite, but I just felt so certain that my ideas were the only ones that made sense. I was interrupting Mr. Henderson, and he's been on the board for twelve years! I just felt this... this surge of confidence, like I had all the answers and everyone else was just moving too slow to keep up with me. 

But then, and this is the strange part, that bright feeling would just turn on a dime. I'd come home from feeling like I owned the room, and the minute I walked through the door, if my husband had left a coffee cup on the counter—just one little cup, mind you—I would just snap at him. I mean, really lay into him over something so small. It was like that energy was a live wire, and sometimes it made me feel grand and in charge, and other times it just made me so irritable I could spit. So, yes, I was overly confident, absolutely, but it wasn't all sunshine, not for the people around me, anyway.
About that unusually energetic period a few months ago, did it last at least four days in a row?

Oh, four days... well, it was definitely longer than that. You see, this whole... this whole shift, the sharper change with the energy and feeling so bold and then snapping at my husband and then the low, cloudy feeling I mentioned before... it's all been going on for about two weeks now. 

And I can tell you exactly why, or at least exactly when it started, because it was right around the time my husband retired. Yes, two weeks ago he had his little send-off at the firm, and suddenly he's just... home. All day. Every day. He's always been a busy man, always out the door by seven, and now he's just sitting in his armchair reading the paper while I'm trying to get things done. 

I think that's what set off this whole stretch of me just buzzing around and feeling so certain about everything, because I had to overcompensate for him just being underfoot. So, yes, it wasn't just a weekend thing. It's been a solid two weeks of this back-and-forth, high-energy, confident, irritable, and then just... crashing into that heavy feeling. Two whole weeks since he started his retirement, bless his heart, but it's really thrown my entire routine out the window, and my mood right along with it.
During that high-energy period, did it cause serious problems at work or at home?

Well, serious problems... I suppose it depends on what you call serious. I mean, the whole place hasn't burned down, thank goodness. I am still getting to work every single day. I haven't missed a morning at the management office, even with my husband just sitting around the house all day now. But, I will admit... I have definitely had to change how I do things lately, just to keep my head above water and make sure I do not make a mess of the association's funds. 

For instance, I've really had to slow down on making any big decisions. Usually I can just look at a proposal and know right away if it's right for the community, but lately, I've been relying heavily on my assistant, Brenda. She is such a sweet girl, been with me for three years now and she really knows her way around the filing cabinets. I have had to ask her to double-check all the vendor details for me. The landscaping contracts, the pool maintenance schedules, the invoices from the plumbers... all of it. I just hand the paperwork over to her and ask her to make sure the numbers actually make sense and that I haven't missed some glaring error. 

And it is not just the vendors, it is the board meetings, too. I actually went ahead and put off a couple of board items that we were supposed to vote on this past Tuesday. We had a whole discussion planned about resurfacing the tennis courts, which is a huge expense for the community, and I just... I moved it to next month's agenda. I made an excuse and told them we needed more time to review the bids, but the honest truth is, I just do not trust my judgment right now. When I was feeling so bold and full of myself a little while ago, I felt like I could do no wrong, and now I am so worried I will make a terrible mistake that I am just dragging my feet on everything. So I am still doing the job, I am still showing up, but I am definitely having to tiptoe around my own decisions so I do not ruin anything.
During that high-energy period, were you talking more than usual or so fast that other people had trouble interrupting you?

Well, talking more than usual... I suppose that depends on who you ask, doesn't it? If you ask my husband, he'd probably say I never stop talking anyway, bless his heart. But no, I don't think I was talking unusually fast or anything like that. I mean, I told you about that meeting with Mr. Henderson, where I was interrupting him and just feeling so sure of myself about the carport paint colors. I was definitely dominating the conversation, taking up all the air in the room, but it wasn't like my words were tumbling out of my mouth at a million miles an hour. 

I wasn't, you know, speaking so fast that people couldn't get a word in edgewise if they really tried. They just didn't try because I was being so forceful! I just felt very strongly about what I was saying. But as for the speed of it, or just chattering on and on without making any sense... no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I just had a lot to say, and I wanted to make sure everyone heard it, especially with all the stress of my husband being home all day now. You'd think a man who worked for forty years would want to find a hobby, maybe take up golf or woodworking, but no, he just wants to read the paper and comment on every little thing I'm doing in the kitchen... anyway, no, my talking speed was just fine, I think.
During that high-energy period, were you taking on a lot more projects or getting far more done than usual?

Oh, projects... yes, actually, I really was. It’s funny you bring that up because usually I’m very methodical. I like to take things one at a time, especially with the association management, because if you mix up the financials for one community with another, well, it’s a disaster waiting to happen. But during that stretch—right around when my husband started his retirement and was just underfoot all day—I just felt this... this incredible drive to get things moving. 

I decided out of nowhere that we needed to overhaul the energy efficiency for several of the communities I manage. Not just one, mind you, but three different properties all at once. I started pulling all these green-energy proposals—solar panels for the clubhouses, LED retrofitting for the streetlights, drought-resistant landscaping, you name it. I was just stacking them up on my desk. And I kept setting up calls and meetings with all these different vendors and contractors, even though my calendar was already completely full with the regular day-to-day operations. 

I mean, I’d be on the phone with a solar guy at 8:00 AM, then squeezing in a Zoom call with a lighting specialist during my lunch break, and then trying to negotiate with a landscaper at 5:30 when I should have been heading home. I just kept piling more and more on my plate. It felt like I could handle it all, like I had this endless reserve of energy to just push all these initiatives through, even though looking back, it was an impossible amount of work for one person to take on all at once. But at the time, I just felt so capable, so determined to get it all done right then and there.
During that high-energy period, did you do anything unusually risky or impulsive, like spending too much money?

Well, spending too much money... I mean, personally, no. I'm very careful with my own checking account, always have been. You kind of have to be when you don't have a lot of formal education to fall back on, you know? But... well, with the association's money... that's a little different, and honestly, it's what has me so tied up in knots right now. 

You see, when I was on that kick with all the energy efficiency projects—the solar panels and the LED lights and all of that—I got a little ahead of myself. I was talking to these vendors, and they were giving me these wonderful pitches about how much money we'd save in the long run, and I just felt so certain that it was the right move. So certain, in fact, that... well, I might have jumped the gun a bit. 

I told a couple of the vendors—the solar guys for the Pine Ridge clubhouse and the lighting contractors for the Oak Creek pathways—I told them to go ahead and hold the equipment for us. I even told them to start drafting up the final paperwork, the contracts and the work orders, before I had actually sat down and really, thoroughly checked the budgets for those specific communities. I just felt like, "Oh, we'll find the money, it's such a good investment, the board will love it." 

But now... now that I've sort of come down from that whole burst of energy, I am just sick with worry about it. I mean, I haven't signed anything final, thank goodness, but I made verbal commitments. I told them we were moving forward. And now I'm looking at the reserve funds for Pine Ridge, and they just had that massive plumbing issue last month that drained a lot of their contingency money, and I am terrified that I've put us in a really bad spot. If these vendors try to hold us to those agreements, or if they charge us restocking fees for the equipment they held... I don't know how I'm going to explain that to the board. It was just so impulsive, which is not like me at all. I usually cross every 't' and dot every 'i' twice over, but I just got so swept up in the idea of getting it all done right that second.
During that high-energy period, did it ever get so severe that you were hospitalized?

Hospitalized? Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I mean, I was certainly running myself ragged, and as I said, I made some very foolish decisions with the vendors that I am still losing sleep over, but it was never anything that would put me in a hospital. I've never been hospitalized for anything like this. 

The only time I've ever really been in the hospital was when I had my gallbladder out back in '98, and even then, I was itching to get back to work because the temp they hired to cover my desk didn't know the first thing about filing the monthly assessment reports. But no, nothing like that for this. I was just... very energized, very focused on getting those projects off the ground. 

I suppose if I had kept going at that pace, maybe I would have collapsed from exhaustion eventually, because I was certainly pushing myself too hard. I mean, between the phone calls and the emails and trying to manage the regular maintenance requests—which never stop, by the way, someone always has a leaky faucet or a complaint about a neighbor's dog barking too loud—it was a lot. But I didn't lose my mind or anything, and I certainly didn't need to be locked away or put under observation. 

I just... I got carried away. I got too big for my britches, thinking I could single-handedly modernize three different properties while my husband was sitting at home complaining about the television volume. But no hospital. I just rode it out until I sort of crashed, and now I'm just dealing with the mess I made. But I'm still going to work every day, still trying to sort it all out, piece by piece.
About that unusually high-energy period, did it last a full week or longer?

Well, a week... yes, definitely longer than a week. It’s been going on for about two weeks now, actually. It all started right around the time my husband officially retired. You know, he worked at the plant for thirty-five years, same shift, same routine, and then suddenly—bam—he's home all day. Every day. Just... there. And right when that happened, I noticed this shift in myself. 

At first, it was that sharp spike in my energy and my confidence, like I was telling you about with the solar panels and the lighting contracts. I just felt like I could conquer the world, or at least modernize every community in the county, and that lasted for a good stretch. I was just buzzing along, feeling so capable, so on top of everything, even with him underfoot asking what was for lunch at 10:30 in the morning. 

But then, after that initial burst, it sort of... morphed. The energy broke, and I dropped into this low, cloudy feeling that I'm stuck in right now. The worry about the budgets, the dread of having to explain myself to the board... it's all just been hanging over me. So, yes, if you look at the whole picture—the sudden high energy, the extreme confidence, and now this awful, cloudy slump—it's been a solid two weeks since his retirement party, and it just hasn't let up. It’s been quite the rollercoaster, let me tell you, and I’m just exhausted from the whole thing.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that my head feels cloudy, like I stare at a board packet or a vendor email and cannot decide even simple things I used to handle fast.
target_item.reason: This is the first turn of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code S031 as per the rules.

patient.answer: Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I... I suppose what brings me in is just this awful feeling in my head lately. It's like my brain is full of cotton wool, or fog, or something. Just completely cloudy. I've been managing properties and homeowner associations for years—decades, really—and I've always been sharp. I had to be, you know? But lately, I'll sit down at my desk, and I'll pull up a board packet for the upcoming monthly meeting, or maybe just a simple email from one of our landscaping vendors asking about the sprinkler schedule, and I just stare at it. I stare at the words and I can't... I just can't make a decision. Things that used to take me two seconds, things I could do in my sleep, are suddenly impossible. I'll read the same paragraph over and over, and my mind just won't process it. It's so frustrating because I know I should be able to handle it, but I just sit there, staring at the screen, completely stuck.

inference.note: Initial broad differential for subjective cognitive clouding and impaired concentration/decision-making includes depressive episode/recurrent depression, anxiety/stress-related conditions, other neurotic disorder, unspecified mental disorder due to known physiological condition, and mild cognitive impairment.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the cognitive fog is occurring in the context of depressed mood, helping distinguish a depressive disorder from primary anxiety, adjustment, or neurocognitive causes.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling down or depressed, which corresponds to Depressed Mood. My symptom profile does not include a specific symptom key for Depressed Mood, although it includes related symptoms like Loss of Interest and Worthlessness/Guilt.

patient.answer:
Depressed... well, I don't really know if I'd call it that. I just... I'm not sure. I mean, I guess I feel bad about myself, but wouldn't anyone in my shoes? It’s just... well, let me explain it like this. I’ve been working since I was a young girl. I didn't even make it past the eighth grade, you know, I had to go right out and work to help my family, and I built my whole life up from nothing. I worked my way up to where I am now, and I’m proud of that. I handle huge budgets and important decisions for these communities. 

So when I sit at my desk and I can't even figure out if we should approve a simple, everyday repair for a community pool gate... it’s upsetting. It really is. I just sit there and wonder what on earth is wrong with me. I don't know if that means I'm depressed in the medical way you doctors mean. I'm just so incredibly frustrated with this cloud in my head. It makes me feel... well, just useless, really. I go home and I just think about all the things I didn't get done. Like yesterday, a resident was asking about her parking spot, and usually I'd just handle it in a snap, but I just stared at the screen, and then I went home and just sat there feeling awful about it all evening. So, am I depressed? I really couldn't tell you for sure. I just know I don't feel right.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective short-term memory impairment suggestive of a neurocognitive disorder rather than primarily depression, anxiety, or adjustment-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: Have you been forgetting recent conversations or appointments?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory loss or forgetfulness, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, it's not like that. I'm not forgetting things. My memory is fine, thank goodness. I mean, I can still remember all the bylaws for the different associations I manage, and I know exactly who called me yesterday and what they said. Like Mrs. Higgins in unit 4B, she called about her neighbor's dog barking again, and I remember every word of that conversation. And my appointments, well, I have my calendar right there on my desk, but I don't even really need to look at it most days. I know when my meetings are. 

It's just... it's the *doing* of the things that's the problem. I remember that I need to call the roofer about the leak at the Oakwood property, I know the appointment is at 2:00 PM, I remember the conversation I had with the board president about it, but when the time comes to actually pick up the phone and make the decision on the estimate... that's when the fog rolls in. I just sit there. So the memory is all there, clear as a bell. It's just the rest of my brain that feels like it's wading through molasses. I'll remember that I sat there for an hour getting nothing done, which just makes me feel worse, you know? But no, no lost time or forgotten conversations. Just this awful inability to act on what I remember.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient is experiencing anhedonia, which would help distinguish a depressive disorder from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or non-depressive cognitive/executive complaints.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I have not wanted to go to my dance class, look at the little galleries, or cook Sunday food for my family, and those are things that usually make me feel like myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about losing interest or pleasure in usually enjoyed activities, which matches this symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. And that's another thing that's been bothering me so much. You see, I've always been a very active person outside of work, too. For years, I've gone to this wonderful little dance class on Thursday evenings. It's just a local group, mostly ladies my age, and we do a bit of everything—some line dancing, a little ballroom, just moving around and having a good time. It’s always been the highlight of my week. I’d get off work, maybe grab a quick bite, and head straight there. But lately... I just can't bring myself to go. The thought of putting on my shoes and driving over there just feels like climbing a mountain. I haven't been in weeks. 

And it's not just the dancing. On the weekends, I usually love to stroll downtown and look at the little art galleries. I don't always buy anything, but I love seeing what the local artists are doing, chatting with the gallery owners—I know most of them by name now. It’s a lovely way to spend a Saturday afternoon. But now, the idea of getting dressed and walking around just seems exhausting. I’d rather just sit in my chair at home. 

Even Sunday dinners... oh, that's the hardest part. I've always cooked a big Sunday meal for my family. My kids and grandkids come over, and I make a roast, or sometimes a big pot of my mother's famous chicken and dumplings. I love the house smelling like good food, hearing everyone laughing in the living room while I’m finishing up the gravy. It's what makes me feel like *me*, you know? The matriarch, taking care of everyone. But the last few Sundays, I've just told them I wasn't up to it. I couldn't even fathom the idea of planning a menu, going to the grocery store, standing at the stove for hours... It just feels so heavy. So, yes, I suppose I have lost interest. All the things that usually bring me joy, that make me feel alive and like myself... they just feel like chores now, and I just don't have the energy or the desire for them anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine whether psychomotor slowing/fatigue is present to better distinguish a depressive episode from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or non-depressive cognitive conditions.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling slowed down physically, like your body is moving through molasses?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: At home I move slow like my legs are heavy, but in meetings I catch myself tapping my pen, shifting in the chair, and feeling too keyed up to sit still.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling physically slowed down, which refers to psychomotor retardation, a component of psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Well, it's funny you should put it exactly that way, because yes, sometimes I do feel just like that—like I'm moving through molasses. But it's not all the time, and that's what makes it so confusing for me. 

When I'm at home, especially in the evenings after work or on those weekends when I just can't bring myself to go out to the galleries, it's like my legs are made of lead. Getting up from my chair in the living room to just go to the kitchen for a glass of water feels like such an enormous effort. I move so slowly, dragging my feet across the carpet, and I just feel physically heavy. I'll tell myself, 'Come on, just stand up,' and it takes me five minutes to actually do it. It's like my body just doesn't want to cooperate with what little bit of will I have left. 

But then... then there are other times, mostly at work, where it's the exact opposite. And this is what I don't understand. I'll be in one of those board meetings—you know, the ones where we have to discuss the annual budgets or deal with a difficult contractor—and I just can't seem to settle down. I'll be sitting there, and I catch myself tapping my pen on the notepad, just tap-tap-tap, until one of the board members gives me a look. Or I'm shifting my weight in the chair, crossing and uncrossing my legs, adjusting my posture every two minutes. I feel so keyed up, almost like there's an electric current running under my skin, and I just can't sit still to save my life. It's not a good kind of energy, though; it's this uncomfortable, restless feeling. 

So it's both, really. Heavy and slow like molasses when I'm alone in my house, but then all jittery and wound up tight when I'm trying to sit through a meeting. It makes no sense to me. How can a person be too exhausted to walk to the kitchen, but too restless to sit in a chair at the office? It's just exhausting in a whole different way, dealing with this back-and-forth.

inference.note: Psychomotor change is now endorsed, with both retardation at home and agitation/restlessness at work. Along with anhedonia and impaired concentration/indecisiveness, this strengthens a depressive episode/recurrent depression. Preserved memory keeps F09/G31.84 less favored but not excluded yet. No change to candidate list until duration, sleep, appetite, guilt, suicidality, and episodicity are clarified.

doctor.intent: Assess suicidal ideation to determine severity and support major depressive episode vs anxiety/adjustment disorders.
doctor.question: Have you been having thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: A few mornings I have had the scary thought that maybe it would be easier if I just did not wake up, but I do not want to hurt myself and I have no plan.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of life not being worth living or thoughts of self-harm, which maps directly to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens... that’s... well, that’s a very hard question to hear out loud. But, to be completely honest with you, because I know I need to be... there have been a few mornings lately. 

You know, it's usually right when the sun is just starting to peek through the gaps in the blinds in my bedroom, right before my alarm is even set to go off. I’ll just be lying there, looking up at the ceiling fan, thinking about everything I have to do that day—the emails from the association board, the contractors I need to wrangle, and just the sheer effort of putting my feet on the floor. And... well, I’ve had this really scary thought creep in. Just a flash, really, but it frightens me so much. I catch myself thinking that maybe... maybe it would just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. If I could just stay asleep and not have to face the day or this awful, heavy feeling anymore. 

It terrifies me to even admit that to you, because I’ve always been such a strong person, you know? I'm the one holding it all together, the matriarch, like I said. But I need you to know—and I tell myself this right after the thought happens—I do not want to hurt myself. Oh, Lord, no. I could never, ever do that. I think about my kids, and my grandchildren, and the thought of leaving them that way, of putting them through that kind of pain... it breaks my heart to even imagine it. So, no, I don't have any sort of plan or anything like that. I'm not going to do anything to harm myself, I promise you that. It's just... it's just that fleeting, frightening wish that I could just peacefully not wake up, just so I wouldn't have to push through the day anymore.

inference.note: Passive death wish and prior symptoms (anhedonia, psychomotor change, impaired concentration/indecisiveness) strengthen a depressive syndrome; cognitive disorders F09 and G31.84 are less likely given preserved memory and the executive problem occurring in the context of mood symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms have been present most of the day, nearly every day for at least two weeks, which would strongly support a major depressive episode over anxiety or adjustment-related diagnoses.
doctor.question: Have these problems been going on for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This sharper change in my energy, confidence, and then the low cloudy feeling has been going on for about two weeks, since my husband retired and was suddenly home all day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the current symptoms have been present for at least two weeks, which matches the duration profile item.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about the exact timing, because I do try to keep track of when things start feeling off. It’s been... yes, it’s been right around two weeks. I know this for a fact because it all really started to shift right when my husband retired. 

He just officially retired two weeks ago, you see. After all these years of him going off to work every single morning, suddenly he is just... home. All day long. And bless his heart, I love him dearly, we've been married a long time, but having him underfoot from dawn until dusk has been such a huge adjustment. I’m used to having my mornings to myself, getting my association paperwork sorted out at the dining room table in peace, and now he’s wandering around the kitchen asking what’s for lunch at ten in the morning, or sitting in his recliner watching his programs with the volume turned way up. 

It was right around that exact time, two weeks ago, that I noticed this sharper change in myself. At first, I had this shift in my energy and my confidence, like I was trying to manage everything and everyone all at once and feeling so wound up. But then, almost right on the heels of that, came this... this low, cloudy feeling. That heavy, exhausting feeling I was telling you about earlier. So, yes, doctor, it’s been a solid two weeks of this. Ever since he was suddenly home all day, it just feels like my whole routine got turned upside down, and this awful cloudy feeling settled right in over me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are tied to an identifiable stressor and fit an adjustment disorder rather than a primary depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel these symptoms started because of your husband retiring and being home all day?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The depressed stretches have been coming back on and off for about a year, but this latest one feels more tied to what happened after my husband stopped working.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms were triggered by the husband's retirement, which perfectly matches the manifestation for the depressive episode duration where the patient clarifies that while she has had depressed stretches for a year, this latest episode is tied to her husband stopping work.

patient.answer:
Well, now that you ask it quite like that, I suppose I should clarify a bit. I don't want to lay all the blame on my dear husband, heaven knows. It's not quite that simple. 

You see, if I'm being perfectly honest and looking back over the calendar... these low periods, these stretches where everything feels like wading through that molasses I mentioned, they've actually been coming and going for a while now. I'd say it's been happening on and off for about a year. I remember last Thanksgiving feeling just so dreadful and hollow while trying to get the turkey in the oven, and then again around Easter when I couldn't even bring myself to arrange the centerpieces for the association luncheon. So, the cloudy feeling itself isn't entirely new. 

But... and this is the important part, I think... this particular stretch, the one I'm in right now, it definitely feels like it was triggered or maybe just made so much worse by his retirement. It’s like the stress of him suddenly being in my space all day, disrupting my peace and quiet and my routines... it just flipped a switch. So while the depressed stretches have been creeping up on me for a year or so, this latest, heavy bout—the one that's kept me down for the last two weeks—feels entirely tied to the upheaval of him stopping work and being home from dawn to dusk. It just pushed me right back down into that hole, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine whether she has had a past major depressive episode, which would distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder from a single episode or adjustment/anxiety diagnoses.

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the history and duration of past depressive episodes, which corresponds to the patient's history of depressed stretches occurring on and off for about a year.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, absolutely. If I really sit down and look at the calendar, they definitely last that long, if not longer. Like I mentioned a moment ago with Thanksgiving... that wasn't just a bad weekend or a fleeting mood. Oh, heavens no. I felt that awful, heavy way from the very first week of November all the way through to early December. I remember it so clearly because the community association always does a canned food drive right around then, and I am usually the one organizing the collection bins down at the clubhouse, making sure the flyers are distributed to all the units. But last year, I just couldn't muster the energy for weeks on end. I had to have Mrs. Gable from unit 4B handle the whole thing, which I hated doing, but I just couldn't get out of bed some days. 

It was the exact same story around Easter, too. It just dragged on and on for well over a month before the clouds finally parted. So, yes, to answer your question, these depressed stretches, they have been coming back on and off for about a year now, and when they do settle in, they certainly overstay their welcome for at least two weeks, sometimes much longer. 

But I just have to say again, because it's weighing on me so heavily right now... even though this has been happening for a year, this latest one feels so much more tied to what happened after my husband stopped working. It's like the other times were just a terrible season I had to wait out, but this time, him being home all day, asking me questions while I'm trying to balance the association ledger, changing the channel on the television when I'm trying to have a moment of quiet... it just brought the storm right into my living room, if that makes sense. So yes, they do last a long time, but this one just feels so specifically wrapped up in his retirement.

inference.note: History now supports recurrent major depressive episodes lasting >2 weeks over the past year, so F33.1 is added and prioritized over single-episode depression (F32.9). Anxiety disorder remains a differential due to restlessness/tension.

doctor.intent: Determine whether she has ever had a past manic or hypomanic episode, to rule out bipolar spectrum disorder as the cause of recurrent depressive episodes.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually energetic or needed much less sleep than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I had this push in my body like I had to keep moving, calling people, making lists, and walking the properties even after I should have gone home.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about feeling unusually energetic maps directly to the symptom of abnormally and persistently increased energy/activity.

patient.answer:
Well, yes... yes, actually. I don't know if I'd say I needed less sleep, but the energy... oh, heavens, the energy. It was like I had this... this push inside my body, just this constant hum, like I had to keep moving every single second. 

It happened... oh, I guess it was a few months ago now. I was just going a mile a minute. I’d be up and I just couldn't sit still. I was calling everyone on the association board, sometimes two or three times a day, just rapid-fire, going over the landscaping budget, the pool maintenance schedule, making these huge, elaborate lists of every little thing that needed fixing in the whole community. I mean, page after page of lists. And I wouldn't just stop at the paperwork, no. I was out walking the properties, inspecting the common areas, checking the sprinkler heads, looking at the paint on the carports... and I'd be doing this long after I should have just gone home and put my feet up. 

I remember one evening, it must have been past seven o'clock, getting dark, and there I was, marching around the perimeter fence with my clipboard, just feeling like I could keep going all night. It wasn't like this heavy, cloudy feeling at all, it was the exact opposite. Just this driven, almost frantic need to do things, fix things, organize things. I was exhausted underneath it all, I think, but my body just wouldn't get the message to stop. It was quite a change from how I usually am, I must say.

inference.note: Added bipolar-spectrum diagnoses due to a distinct prior period of markedly increased energy/activity and restlessness suggesting hypomanic symptoms; removed F32.9 because recurrent episodes are established, and F41.9 because anxiety alone no longer explains the syndrome. Adjustment disorder remains possible as a trigger for the current exacerbation but is less likely given the year-long recurrent episodes.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about decreased need for sleep, but there is no specific symptom for decreased need for sleep in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask about the sleep specifically, because when I was rushing around like that, making all those lists and checking the sprinkler heads and calling the board members... I honestly can't say for sure if I actually *needed* less sleep. It wasn't like I was staying up until three in the morning baking pies or anything like that. 

I mean, I still went to bed around my usual time, maybe a little later because my mind was just racing with all the things I still had to do for the association, like whether we should switch from pine straw to mulch around the clubhouse. But I don't recall waking up at the crack of dawn feeling completely refreshed on just a few hours of sleep, if that's what you mean. 

It was more that while I was awake, I just couldn't turn the motor off. I was just going and going. But as for the sleep itself... I really don't think I was sleeping significantly less than I usually do. Or at least, I didn't notice it if I was. I was just so focused on getting everything done, you see. I suppose I was probably still getting my normal seven or eight hours, just... tossing and turning a bit more before I finally drifted off. So, no, I don't think the sleep part was really the issue, just the non-stop doing things during the day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior high-energy episode included abnormally elevated or expansive mood, which would help distinguish bipolar spectrum illness from recurrent depression or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During that high-energy period a few months ago, did you feel unusually cheerful or overly confident?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: There were days when I felt almost too bright and bold, talking over people at the association meetings, and then I would snap at my husband over some small thing at home.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I felt unusually cheerful (elevated mood), which maps to S033.

patient.answer:
Well, cheerful is a funny word for it, but... oh, I suppose there were days during that stretch where I felt, I don't know, almost too bright? Too bold, maybe. Like I was just on top of the world and nobody could tell me otherwise. 

I remember at one of the association meetings—it was the one where we were discussing the new paint colors for the carports, which is always a contentious issue, let me tell you—I was just holding court. I was talking over people, which I never do, I'm usually very polite, but I just felt so certain that my ideas were the only ones that made sense. I was interrupting Mr. Henderson, and he's been on the board for twelve years! I just felt this... this surge of confidence, like I had all the answers and everyone else was just moving too slow to keep up with me. 

But then, and this is the strange part, that bright feeling would just turn on a dime. I'd come home from feeling like I owned the room, and the minute I walked through the door, if my husband had left a coffee cup on the counter—just one little cup, mind you—I would just snap at him. I mean, really lay into him over something so small. It was like that energy was a live wire, and sometimes it made me feel grand and in charge, and other times it just made me so irritable I could spit. So, yes, I was overly confident, absolutely, but it wasn't all sunshine, not for the people around me, anyway.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the unusually energetic period, which corresponds to the 'duration' item in the symptom profile that covers the timeline of the changes in energy and confidence.

patient.answer:
Oh, four days... well, it was definitely longer than that. You see, this whole... this whole shift, the sharper change with the energy and feeling so bold and then snapping at my husband and then the low, cloudy feeling I mentioned before... it's all been going on for about two weeks now. 

And I can tell you exactly why, or at least exactly when it started, because it was right around the time my husband retired. Yes, two weeks ago he had his little send-off at the firm, and suddenly he's just... home. All day. Every day. He's always been a busy man, always out the door by seven, and now he's just sitting in his armchair reading the paper while I'm trying to get things done. 

I think that's what set off this whole stretch of me just buzzing around and feeling so certain about everything, because I had to overcompensate for him just being underfoot. So, yes, it wasn't just a weekend thing. It's been a solid two weeks of this back-and-forth, high-energy, confident, irritable, and then just... crashing into that heavy feeling. Two whole weeks since he started his retirement, bless his heart, but it's really thrown my entire routine out the window, and my mood right along with it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable period caused marked impairment or hospitalization, which best distinguishes hypomania (bipolar II) from mania (bipolar I/unspecified bipolar) versus recurrent unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During that high-energy period, did it cause serious problems at work or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I am still getting to work, but I have had to slow down decisions, ask my assistant to double-check vendor details, and put off a couple of board items because I do not trust my judgment right now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the high-energy period caused serious problems at work or home, which relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, serious problems... I suppose it depends on what you call serious. I mean, the whole place hasn't burned down, thank goodness. I am still getting to work every single day. I haven't missed a morning at the management office, even with my husband just sitting around the house all day now. But, I will admit... I have definitely had to change how I do things lately, just to keep my head above water and make sure I do not make a mess of the association's funds. 

For instance, I've really had to slow down on making any big decisions. Usually I can just look at a proposal and know right away if it's right for the community, but lately, I've been relying heavily on my assistant, Brenda. She is such a sweet girl, been with me for three years now and she really knows her way around the filing cabinets. I have had to ask her to double-check all the vendor details for me. The landscaping contracts, the pool maintenance schedules, the invoices from the plumbers... all of it. I just hand the paperwork over to her and ask her to make sure the numbers actually make sense and that I haven't missed some glaring error. 

And it is not just the vendors, it is the board meetings, too. I actually went ahead and put off a couple of board items that we were supposed to vote on this past Tuesday. We had a whole discussion planned about resurfacing the tennis courts, which is a huge expense for the community, and I just... I moved it to next month's agenda. I made an excuse and told them we needed more time to review the bids, but the honest truth is, I just do not trust my judgment right now. When I was feeling so bold and full of myself a little while ago, I felt like I could do no wrong, and now I am so worried I will make a terrible mistake that I am just dragging my feet on everything. So I am still doing the job, I am still showing up, but I am definitely having to tiptoe around my own decisions so I do not ruin anything.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period involved increased talkativeness/pressured speech, which would support hypomania over recurrent unipolar depression and help distinguish bipolar II from major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: During that high-energy period, were you talking more than usual or so fast that other people had trouble interrupting you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about increased talkativeness or pressured speech, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, talking more than usual... I suppose that depends on who you ask, doesn't it? If you ask my husband, he'd probably say I never stop talking anyway, bless his heart. But no, I don't think I was talking unusually fast or anything like that. I mean, I told you about that meeting with Mr. Henderson, where I was interrupting him and just feeling so sure of myself about the carport paint colors. I was definitely dominating the conversation, taking up all the air in the room, but it wasn't like my words were tumbling out of my mouth at a million miles an hour. 

I wasn't, you know, speaking so fast that people couldn't get a word in edgewise if they really tried. They just didn't try because I was being so forceful! I just felt very strongly about what I was saying. But as for the speed of it, or just chattering on and on without making any sense... no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I just had a lot to say, and I wanted to make sure everyone heard it, especially with all the stress of my husband being home all day now. You'd think a man who worked for forty years would want to find a hobby, maybe take up golf or woodworking, but no, he just wants to read the paper and comment on every little thing I'm doing in the kitchen... anyway, no, my talking speed was just fine, I think.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable period included increased goal-directed activity, a key hypomanic symptom that would help distinguish bipolar II/unspecified bipolar from recurrent major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: During that high-energy period, were you taking on a lot more projects or getting far more done than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I took on extra green-energy proposals for several communities at the same time and kept setting up calls and meetings even when my calendar was already full.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks about taking on more projects or getting more done, which directly corresponds to increased goal-directed activity.

patient.answer:
Oh, projects... yes, actually, I really was. It’s funny you bring that up because usually I’m very methodical. I like to take things one at a time, especially with the association management, because if you mix up the financials for one community with another, well, it’s a disaster waiting to happen. But during that stretch—right around when my husband started his retirement and was just underfoot all day—I just felt this... this incredible drive to get things moving. 

I decided out of nowhere that we needed to overhaul the energy efficiency for several of the communities I manage. Not just one, mind you, but three different properties all at once. I started pulling all these green-energy proposals—solar panels for the clubhouses, LED retrofitting for the streetlights, drought-resistant landscaping, you name it. I was just stacking them up on my desk. And I kept setting up calls and meetings with all these different vendors and contractors, even though my calendar was already completely full with the regular day-to-day operations. 

I mean, I’d be on the phone with a solar guy at 8:00 AM, then squeezing in a Zoom call with a lighting specialist during my lunch break, and then trying to negotiate with a landscaper at 5:30 when I should have been heading home. I just kept piling more and more on my plate. It felt like I could handle it all, like I had this endless reserve of energy to just push all these initiatives through, even though looking back, it was an impossible amount of work for one person to take on all at once. But at the time, I just felt so capable, so determined to get it all done right then and there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period included risky or impulsive behavior, which helps distinguish hypomania/bipolar disorder from recurrent unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During that high-energy period, did you do anything unusually risky or impulsive, like spending too much money?

target_item.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I told a couple of vendors to go ahead and hold equipment or start paperwork before I had really checked the budgets, and now I am worried I put us in a bad spot.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about risky or impulsive behaviors with potential negative consequences, such as spending too much money, which matches the symptom of painful consequence behavior.

patient.answer:
Well, spending too much money... I mean, personally, no. I'm very careful with my own checking account, always have been. You kind of have to be when you don't have a lot of formal education to fall back on, you know? But... well, with the association's money... that's a little different, and honestly, it's what has me so tied up in knots right now. 

You see, when I was on that kick with all the energy efficiency projects—the solar panels and the LED lights and all of that—I got a little ahead of myself. I was talking to these vendors, and they were giving me these wonderful pitches about how much money we'd save in the long run, and I just felt so certain that it was the right move. So certain, in fact, that... well, I might have jumped the gun a bit. 

I told a couple of the vendors—the solar guys for the Pine Ridge clubhouse and the lighting contractors for the Oak Creek pathways—I told them to go ahead and hold the equipment for us. I even told them to start drafting up the final paperwork, the contracts and the work orders, before I had actually sat down and really, thoroughly checked the budgets for those specific communities. I just felt like, "Oh, we'll find the money, it's such a good investment, the board will love it." 

But now... now that I've sort of come down from that whole burst of energy, I am just sick with worry about it. I mean, I haven't signed anything final, thank goodness, but I made verbal commitments. I told them we were moving forward. And now I'm looking at the reserve funds for Pine Ridge, and they just had that massive plumbing issue last month that drained a lot of their contingency money, and I am terrified that I've put us in a really bad spot. If these vendors try to hold us to those agreements, or if they charge us restocking fees for the equipment they held... I don't know how I'm going to explain that to the board. It was just so impulsive, which is not like me at all. I usually cross every 't' and dot every 'i' twice over, but I just got so swept up in the idea of getting it all done right that second.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable period caused marked social or occupational impairment, which would distinguish mania (bipolar I) from hypomania (bipolar II) and recurrent major depression.
doctor.question: During that high-energy period, did it ever get so severe that you were hospitalized?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hospitalization during the high-energy period, which is not covered by any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Hospitalized? Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I mean, I was certainly running myself ragged, and as I said, I made some very foolish decisions with the vendors that I am still losing sleep over, but it was never anything that would put me in a hospital. I've never been hospitalized for anything like this. 

The only time I've ever really been in the hospital was when I had my gallbladder out back in '98, and even then, I was itching to get back to work because the temp they hired to cover my desk didn't know the first thing about filing the monthly assessment reports. But no, nothing like that for this. I was just... very energized, very focused on getting those projects off the ground. 

I suppose if I had kept going at that pace, maybe I would have collapsed from exhaustion eventually, because I was certainly pushing myself too hard. I mean, between the phone calls and the emails and trying to manage the regular maintenance requests—which never stop, by the way, someone always has a leaky faucet or a complaint about a neighbor's dog barking too loud—it was a lot. But I didn't lose my mind or anything, and I certainly didn't need to be locked away or put under observation. 

I just... I got carried away. I got too big for my britches, thinking I could single-handedly modernize three different properties while my husband was sitting at home complaining about the television volume. But no hospital. I just rode it out until I sort of crashed, and now I'm just dealing with the mess I made. But I'm still going to work every day, still trying to sort it all out, piece by piece.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period met the full one-week duration threshold for mania versus the four-day threshold for hypomania, to distinguish bipolar I/bipolar unspecified from bipolar II and recurrent major depression.
doctor.question: About that unusually high-energy period, did it last a full week or longer?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This sharper change in my energy, confidence, and then the low cloudy feeling has been going on for about two weeks, since my husband retired and was suddenly home all day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the high-energy period, which matches the 'duration' profile detailing how long these changes have been going on.

patient.answer:
Well, a week... yes, definitely longer than a week. It’s been going on for about two weeks now, actually. It all started right around the time my husband officially retired. You know, he worked at the plant for thirty-five years, same shift, same routine, and then suddenly—bam—he's home all day. Every day. Just... there. And right when that happened, I noticed this shift in myself. 

At first, it was that sharp spike in my energy and my confidence, like I was telling you about with the solar panels and the lighting contracts. I just felt like I could conquer the world, or at least modernize every community in the county, and that lasted for a good stretch. I was just buzzing along, feeling so capable, so on top of everything, even with him underfoot asking what was for lunch at 10:30 in the morning. 

But then, after that initial burst, it sort of... morphed. The energy broke, and I dropped into this low, cloudy feeling that I'm stuck in right now. The worry about the budgets, the dread of having to explain myself to the board... it's all just been hanging over me. So, yes, if you look at the whole picture—the sudden high energy, the extreme confidence, and now this awful, cloudy slump—it's been a solid two weeks since his retirement party, and it just hasn't let up. It’s been quite the rollercoaster, let me tell you, and I’m just exhausted from the whole thing.
